questions.q: A patient develops polyuria and polydipsia after surgery that damages the hypothalamo-neurohypophyseal tract. Which hormone deficiency most directly accounts for the symptoms?
questions.explain: Antidiuretic hormone (vasopressin) is synthesised in hypothalamic nuclei and transported down axons for storage and release from the posterior pituitary. Deficiency reduces collecting-duct water reabsorption and causes central diabetes insipidus.

questions.q: A hypothalamic lesion interrupts delivery of hypophysiotropic hormones through the hypophyseal portal circulation. Which anterior pituitary hormone would be expected to increase because its secretion is normally under tonic hypothalamic inhibition?
questions.explain: Dopamine from the hypothalamus tonically inhibits prolactin secretion from anterior pituitary lactotrophs. Interruption of hypothalamic delivery removes this inhibition and can cause hyperprolactinaemia.

questions.q: A rise in circulating IGF-1 after growth hormone administration normally feeds back to reduce further growth hormone secretion. Which site contributes to this negative feedback?
questions.explain: IGF-1 exerts negative feedback at the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary, reducing GHRH drive and growth hormone release while favouring somatostatin.

questions.q: A patient with primary hypothyroidism has low free T4. Which pattern of pituitary TSH is expected when the hypothalamic-pituitary axis is intact?
questions.explain: Reduced thyroid hormone removes negative feedback on the hypothalamus and anterior pituitary. In primary thyroid failure, TSH therefore rises.

questions.q: Which stimulus is the most potent physiological trigger for antidiuretic hormone release in a healthy adult?
options: Increased blood glucose after a meal
questions.explain: Hypothalamic osmoreceptors detect small increases in plasma osmolality and stimulate ADH secretion. A sufficiently large fall in effective circulating volume is also a powerful stimulus.
